Tier A analysis · Fisher's Iris, 150 specimens

The leaderboard is measuring the split

What the most-used dataset in machine learning can and cannot tell you about choosing a model.

Prepared for the data science team lead · Source: Kaggle Iris.csv (Anderson 1935 / Fisher 1936, via UCI) · 150 specimens, 4 measurements, 3 species · Full pipeline in notebooks 01–06

Executive summary

SituationFisher's 1936 Iris table is the most-used dataset in the history of statistics and machine learning, and the first exercise nearly every analyst ever runs. Its standard output is a leaderboard: eight model families, all landing between 93.9% and 97.9%.
ComplicationThat leaderboard does not survive its own error bars. Holding the model and the data fixed and changing only the split seed moves accuracy 13.3 points — 3.3× the 4.0-point spread between the model families themselves. Meanwhile the file contains an identifier that predicts the label, two transcription errors and a duplicate pair, none of which the standard workflow notices.
ResolutionStop ranking models on this sample size and ship what the data can actually support: one measurement, one threshold rule, and a stated detection floor.
On 150 specimens the leaderboard is measuring the split rather than the model — so the defensible outputs are a one-measurement rule that scores 96.1% and a detection floor that says when an accuracy claim is worth believing.
  1. InstrumentThe file everyone trusts carries three defects that no completeness check can see: the Id column predicts species at 98.7% because the rows are sorted, two documented transcription errors fabricate a duplicate specimen, and a genuine duplicate pair straddles the train/test boundary in two of every three random splits. Only the first changes a result — and it does not degrade one, it manufactures one.
  2. SignalPetals carry the information and one measurement carries nearly all of it: petal width alone scores 96.1% against 97.9% for all four features and 79.7% for sepals alone. Seven engineered features add 0.37 points — indistinguishable from zero.
  3. LimitsNo clear winner survives its own error bar: 5 of 7 rival families cannot be told apart from the best, the detection floor at this sample size is 3.2 points against a 4.0-point spread, and only 19 of 150 specimens are ever misclassified — three of them by every model. The leaderboard is an argument about 19 flowers.

Recommendation — for the data science team lead

  1. Change what the Iris onboarding exercise asks for. Replace “maximise test accuracy” with “defend whether your winner is distinguishable”: a repeated-CV mean with a paired corrected interval against a stated baseline, never a single-split leaderboard.
  2. Adopt the detection-floor table as a review gate. Any accuracy claim smaller than the tabulated minimum for its sample size is returned to the author. At n=150 that floor is 3.2 points; at n=50 it is 7.5.
  3. Add two checks to the ingestion template. Test every monotonic identifier against the target before dismissing it as an index, and count duplicate rows before splitting. Both failures here pass every null-and-range check.
  4. Ship the ruler rule for the botanical answer. Petal width < 0.6 cm → setosa; < 1.6 cm → versicolor; otherwise virginica. Costs 3.8 points against the best model and needs no software.

Part I · Instrument

Three defects hide behind a file with zero missing values

Every completeness check this file can be given, it passes: no nulls, no type errors, no out-of-range values, no violated business rules — 16 of 16 validation rules clear. That is a statement about completeness, and it is silent about correctness. Three defects sit underneath it, and one of them would break a real pipeline.

What the defects actually cost

The full bake-off was re-run on a deduplicated copy and an errata-corrected copy. Reporting this honestly matters more than the forensics themselves:

Random forest95.1795.0995.170.08
SVM (RBF)95.5795.795.570.13
k-NN95.094.995.030.13
Cross-validated accuracy (%) under each treatment of the data defects. Source: Kaggle Iris.csv, 5-fold x 20-repeat stratified CV.

The duplicates and the errata change nothing measurable — the largest shift across five model families is 0.14 points, roughly 23× smaller than the 3.2-point detection floor. They are a correctness problem worth knowing about, not a performance problem. The Id leak is the one that bites, and the asymmetry is the lesson: two of these defects would have cost a real project nothing, while the third would have shipped a model that knew nothing.

Part II · Signal

Petals carry the information, and one measurement carries most of it

The issue tree splits four features into sepal morphology and petal morphology. The split resolves decisively, and then keeps resolving further than expected: not only do petals beat sepals, but a single petal measurement comes within 1.8 points of using all four.

The engineered features do not help — measured, not assumed

The project's analysis notes propose seven derived features and predict that petal area and the petal length:width ratio are “the two most likely to improve model performance”, while correctly asking for the test rather than assuming the answer. Here is the test:

feature_setLDALogistic
Raw 4 features97.9395.43
Raw 4 + all 7 derived98.397.47
Derived only (7)97.497.5
PetalArea alone96.3795.6
PetalLengthWidthRatio alone71.1775.63
Cross-validated accuracy (%) by feature set, identical 100 folds. Source: Kaggle Iris.csv.

Adding all seven moves LDA by +0.37 points and logistic regression by +2.03, and neither is distinguishable from zero under the corrected test (p = 0.59 and p = 0.11). The mechanism was already visible: the two petal columns correlate at ρ = 0.94 and Fisher's first discriminant carries 99.1% of the separation, so the problem has one useful dimension and no product or ratio of four features can manufacture a second. Ratios can actively destroy it — petal length divided by petal width scores just 71.2% alone, because the division cancels the size axis that does the work.

Part III · Limits

The differences everyone reports are at or below the noise floor

Eight model families, one fixed set of 100 folds, hyperparameters tuned in an inner loop so tuning never leaks. The result is not that all models are equal — the same protocol separates petal-only from sepal-only without difficulty. It is that the model-family differences sit right at the edge of what this sample size can resolve.

Worth naming plainly: LDA — the method Fisher invented for this exact dataset in 1936 — posts the best score of all nine estimators, and it still cannot be declared the winner over most of the field. If the best-supported candidate on the most-studied dataset in existence cannot clear its own error bar, a two-point claim on a 300-row project cannot either.

And the number that looks most convincing is the least informative

The held-out set — one stratified 20% cut, touched exactly once — returned 100.0% accuracy. Its 95% Wilson interval is [88.6%, 100.0%], a width of 11.4 points — nearly three times the entire spread between all eight model families. “LDA achieves 100% on held-out data” is true, publishable, and fully compatible with the model's real accuracy being 89%. That single sentence is the whole report in miniature.

Appendix

Methodology, provenance and limitations

A.1 Provenance

This file did not come from Fisher. It came down a four-step chain, and errors entered partway along it: Anderson (1935) collected 150 specimens on the Gaspé Peninsula, Quebec → Fisher (1936) published the table in The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems → the UCI ML Repository digitised it, and its own documentation records two erroneous rows → Kaggle Iris.csv, this file, with an added Id column. SHA-256 logged at ingestion.

A.2 Corrections to the project's analysis notes

The notes in DOCS/Iris_Dataset_Analysis.md are accurate on distributions — the §5 summary table reproduces exactly. Six claims were tested; four did not survive.

Claim in the notesVerified verdict
§2 — Id has “zero information value”Refuted, and inverted. Species occupy contiguous Id blocks; a tree on Id alone scores 98.7%.
§2 — “no duplicates”Refuted. Three duplicate rows on the four measurements: Ids 10/35/38 and 102/143.
§1 — data quality “clean”True for completeness, false at the value level. Rows 35 and 38 carry the documented UCI errata, which is what creates the 10/35/38 collision.
§7 — petal area and petal L:W ratio “most likely to improve performance”Not materially. All seven derived features move LDA +0.37 points, inside one fold's SD. The notes asked for the test rather than assuming; this is the answer.
§6 — “93–100% accuracy depending on model”Reproduced (93.9%–97.9%), but incomplete. The range conceals that the differences within it are at the detection floor.
§2 — setosa linearly separable, versicolor/virginica notConfirmed, and now proved rather than asserted. A hard-margin linear SVM separates setosa with zero training errors on petals alone; versicolor/virginica strands 2 specimens even with all four features and full knowledge of the labels.
 Every correction is evidenced in Notebooks 01–05.

A.3 Protocol

5-fold x 20 repeats stratified CV (100 identical folds), identical folds for every model, so all comparisons are paired. Hyperparameters (k, tree depth, SVM C and gamma) tuned by GridSearchCV in an inner 3-fold loop, so tuning never leaks into a reported score. Scalers, threshold cuts and all tuning are fitted on training folds only. Significance uses the corrected-resampled t-test (Nadeau & Bengio), which inflates the variance by 1/(k·r) + n_test/n_train to account for folds sharing training data; the naive fold bootstrap is reported alongside only to show that it is 5× too narrow. RANDOM_STATE = 42 throughout.

A.4 Assumption checks

Tested before the tests they license, not after. Normality (Shapiro–Wilk) fails in 2 of 12 feature×species groups and equal variance (Levene) on 3 of 4 features, so non-parametric tests lead throughout and parametric ones are reported alongside for comparability. All 12 pairwise comparisons survive Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction at q < 0.05 — which is itself the point: significance discriminates nothing here, and the ranking comes entirely from effect sizes.

A.5 Scope, and what this analysis cannot support

  • Path C (causal) is out of scope and was never attempted. There are no genetic, environmental or temporal variables, and petal width is not an intervention anyone can assign. “Why do the species differ?” is unanswerable from this file.
  • Sampling frame, not a population. All 150 specimens come from one collector, one region, one season, with two of the three species taken from the same pasture on the same day. Every finding is scoped to these specimens; nothing licenses a claim about Iris as a genus, and the ruler rule would need refitting on any other population.
  • Fairness audit: not applicable, with reason. The pipeline's cross-cutting standard makes an audit mandatory for any model affecting people. This one classifies flowers — no protected attribute exists and no person is scored. Recorded as answered rather than skipped. The representation-bias check that does apply was executed and is stated above.
  • No deployment claim. A 90-year-old, single-site, 150-specimen sample cannot support a deployed taxonomic classifier. The transferable outputs are the method and the detection floor.
  • The MDD table is a simulation calibrated to Iris's per-species covariance structure, not a universal constant. It transfers to problems with similar class separation; a harder problem at the same n will have a higher floor.

A.6 Reproducibility

Six numbered notebooks run in order from the raw CSV: ingestion → cleaning and forensics → EDA → diagnostic → modelling → this report. No local module imports, so a fresh clone runs on the pinned dependencies alone. Every number in this report is read from reports/_key_figures.json and the CSV artefacts written by Notebooks 03–05 — nothing here is hardcoded, and the report cannot drift from the analysis.

Every figure in this report was generated by the accompanying notebooks and every number is read from their saved artefacts. Analysis type: descriptive → diagnostic → predictive (Path A then Path B). Causal inference explicitly out of scope.
